cards.q: What is a gravitational field?
cards.a: A region in which a mass experiences a force, without contact.

cards.q: Define gravitational field strength at a point.
cards.a: The force per unit mass on a small mass placed at that point: g=Fm\displaystyle g = \frac{F}{m}g=mF​. Unit: N kg−1\displaystyle \text{N kg}^{-1}N kg−1.

cards.q: State Newton's law of gravitation.
cards.a: The gravitational force between two point masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: F=Gm1m2r2\displaystyle F = \frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}F=r2Gm1​m2​​. It is always attractive.

cards.q: State the unit of the gravitational constant G\displaystyle GG.
cards.a: N m2 kg−2\displaystyle \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-2}N m2 kg−2
cards.why: Rearranging F=Gm1m2r2\displaystyle F = \frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}F=r2Gm1​m2​​ gives G=Fr2m1m2\displaystyle G = \frac{Fr^{2}}{m_{1}m_{2}}G=m1​m2​Fr2​.

cards.q: Calculate the gravitational force between the Earth (mass 5.97×1024 kg\displaystyle 5.97 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}5.97×1024 kg, radius 6.37×106 m\displaystyle 6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}6.37×106 m) and a 70 kg person on its surface. (G=6.67×10−11 N m2 kg−2\displaystyle G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-2}G=6.67×10−11 N m2 kg−2)
cards.a: 690 N
cards.why: This is the person's weight: the same as mg\displaystyle mgmg.
steps: The separation is the distance between centres: the Earth's radius.

F=Gm1m2r2=6.67×10−11×5.97×1024×70(6.37×106)2\displaystyle F = \frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}} = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.97 \times 10^{24} \times 70}{(6.37 \times 10^{6})^{2}}F=r2Gm1​m2​​=(6.37×106)26.67×10−11×5.97×1024×70​
F=690 N\displaystyle F = 690\ \text{N}F=690 N

cards.q: A satellite orbits 400 km above the Earth's surface. A student uses r=400 km\displaystyle r = 400\ \text{km}r=400 km in F=Gm1m2r2\displaystyle F = \frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}F=r2Gm1​m2​​. What is wrong?
cards.a: r\displaystyle rr is the distance between the centres of the two masses. It should be the Earth's radius plus the height: 6.37×106+0.40×106=6.77×106 m\displaystyle 6.37 \times 10^{6} + 0.40 \times 10^{6} = 6.77 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}6.37×106+0.40×106=6.77×106 m.

cards.q: Derive the expression for the gravitational field strength at a distance r\displaystyle rr from a point mass M\displaystyle MM.
cards.a: g=GMr2\displaystyle g = \frac{GM}{r^{2}}g=r2GM​
steps: The force on a small mass m\displaystyle mm at distance r\displaystyle rr is F=GMmr2\displaystyle F = \frac{GMm}{r^{2}}F=r2GMm​.
Field strength is force per unit mass: g=Fm\displaystyle g = \frac{F}{m}g=mF​.
So g=GMr2\displaystyle g = \frac{GM}{r^{2}}g=r2GM​.

cards.q: Calculate the gravitational field strength 400 km above the Earth's surface. (GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1\displaystyle GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1 for the Earth; radius 6.37×106 m\displaystyle 6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}6.37×106 m)
cards.a: 8.7 N kg−1\displaystyle 8.7\ \text{N kg}^{-1}8.7 N kg−1
cards.why: Still about 90% of its surface value: astronauts in orbit are not beyond gravity.
steps: Distance from the centre: r=6.37×106+0.40×106=6.77×106 m\displaystyle r = 6.37 \times 10^{6} + 0.40 \times 10^{6} = 6.77 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}r=6.37×106+0.40×106=6.77×106 m.
g=GMr2=3.98×1014(6.77×106)2\displaystyle g = \frac{GM}{r^{2}} = \frac{3.98 \times 10^{14}}{(6.77 \times 10^{6})^{2}}g=r2GM​=(6.77×106)23.98×1014​
g=8.7 N kg−1\displaystyle g = 8.7\ \text{N kg}^{-1}g=8.7 N kg−1

cards.q: The distance from the centre of a planet doubles. How does the gravitational field strength change?
cards.a: It falls to one quarter: field strength follows an inverse-square law.
cards.why: Writing only that it "decreases with distance" does not earn the mark: say inverse-square.

cards.q: Describe the gravitational field lines around a planet, and close to its surface.
cards.a: Around the planet: radial, pointing towards its centre, and further apart at greater distances. Close to the surface: parallel and equally spaced, showing a uniform field.

cards.q: Define gravitational potential at a point.
cards.a: The work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point. Unit: J kg−1\displaystyle \text{J kg}^{-1}J kg−1.

cards.q: Why is gravitational potential always negative?
cards.a: Potential is defined as zero at infinity. Gravity is attractive, so work must be done on a mass to move it out to infinity: everywhere closer has less potential than zero.

cards.q: Write the equation for the gravitational potential at a distance r\displaystyle rr from a point mass M\displaystyle MM.
cards.a: V=−GMr\displaystyle V = -\frac{GM}{r}V=−rGM​
cards.why: Potential varies as 1r\displaystyle \frac{1}{r}r1​, not 1r2\displaystyle \frac{1}{r^{2}}r21​.

cards.q: Calculate the gravitational potential at the Earth's surface. (GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1\displaystyle GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1; radius 6.37×106 m\displaystyle 6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}6.37×106 m)
cards.a: −6.2×107 J kg−1\displaystyle -6.2 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}−6.2×107 J kg−1
cards.why: Keep the minus sign in the answer.
steps: V=−GMr=−3.98×10146.37×106\displaystyle V = -\frac{GM}{r} = -\frac{3.98 \times 10^{14}}{6.37 \times 10^{6}}V=−rGM​=−6.37×1063.98×1014​
V=−6.2×107 J kg−1\displaystyle V = -6.2 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}V=−6.2×107 J kg−1

cards.q: A 400 kg satellite is moved from a point where the gravitational potential is −6.25×107 J kg−1\displaystyle -6.25 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}−6.25×107 J kg−1 to one where it is −5.00×107 J kg−1\displaystyle -5.00 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}−5.00×107 J kg−1. Calculate the work done.
cards.a: 5.0×109 J\displaystyle 5.0 \times 10^{9}\ \text{J}5.0×109 J
steps: Change in potential: ΔV=−5.00×107−(−6.25×107)=1.25×107 J kg−1\displaystyle \Delta V = -5.00 \times 10^{7} - (-6.25 \times 10^{7}) = 1.25 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}ΔV=−5.00×107−(−6.25×107)=1.25×107 J kg−1.
W=mΔV=400×1.25×107\displaystyle W = m\Delta V = 400 \times 1.25 \times 10^{7}W=mΔV=400×1.25×107
W=5.0×109 J\displaystyle W = 5.0 \times 10^{9}\ \text{J}W=5.0×109 J

cards.q: What is an equipotential surface, and how much work is done moving a mass along one?
cards.a: A surface on which the potential is the same everywhere. No work is done moving a mass along it.
cards.why: Equipotentials are always at right angles to field lines.

cards.q: How is the gravitational field strength found from a graph of potential V\displaystyle VV against distance r\displaystyle rr?
cards.a: It is minus the gradient: g=−ΔVΔr\displaystyle g = -\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta r}g=−ΔrΔV​.

cards.q: What does the area under a graph of gravitational field strength g\displaystyle gg against distance r\displaystyle rr represent?
cards.a: The change in gravitational potential between the two distances.

cards.q: Describe how g\displaystyle gg and V\displaystyle VV vary with distance r\displaystyle rr from the centre of a planet, outside the planet.
cards.a: g\displaystyle gg falls as 1r2\displaystyle \frac{1}{r^{2}}r21​: a steep curve that approaches zero. V\displaystyle VV is negative and rises towards zero as −1r\displaystyle -\frac{1}{r}−r1​: a shallower curve.

cards.q: Derive an expression for the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r\displaystyle rr around a planet of mass M\displaystyle MM.
cards.a: v=GMr\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}v=rGM​​
cards.why: The satellite's own mass cancels: every satellite at that radius has the same speed.
steps: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMmr2=mv2r\displaystyle \frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}r2GMm​=rmv2​.
Cancel m\displaystyle mm and one r\displaystyle rr: v2=GMr\displaystyle v^{2} = \frac{GM}{r}v2=rGM​.
v=GMr\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}v=rGM​​

cards.q: Show that, for a satellite in a circular orbit, T2∝r3\displaystyle T^{2} \propto r^{3}T2∝r3.
cards.a: T2=4π2GMr3\displaystyle T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM}r^{3}T2=GM4π2​r3
steps: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMmr2=mω2r\displaystyle \frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = m\omega^{2}rr2GMm​=mω2r.
Substitute ω=2πT\displaystyle \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}ω=T2π​: GMr2=4π2rT2\displaystyle \frac{GM}{r^{2}} = \frac{4\pi^{2}r}{T^{2}}r2GM​=T24π2r​.
Rearrange: T2=4π2GMr3\displaystyle T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM}r^{3}T2=GM4π2​r3.
4π2GM\displaystyle \frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM}GM4π2​ is constant for a given planet, so T2∝r3\displaystyle T^{2} \propto r^{3}T2∝r3.

cards.q: Calculate the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius 6.77×106 m\displaystyle 6.77 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}6.77×106 m around the Earth. (GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1\displaystyle GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1)
cards.a: 7.7×103 m s−1\displaystyle 7.7 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}7.7×103 m s−1
steps: v=GMr=3.98×10146.77×106\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{3.98 \times 10^{14}}{6.77 \times 10^{6}}}v=rGM​​=6.77×1063.98×1014​​
v=7.7×103 m s−1\displaystyle v = 7.7 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}v=7.7×103 m s−1

cards.q: Calculate the radius of a geostationary orbit around the Earth. (GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1\displaystyle GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1; period 24 hours)
cards.a: 4.2×107 m\displaystyle 4.2 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}4.2×107 m
cards.why: This is measured from the centre of the Earth: about 36 000 km above the surface.
steps: Period: T=24×3600=86 400 s\displaystyle T = 24 \times 3600 = 86\,400\ \text{s}T=24×3600=86400 s.

From T2=4π2r3GM\displaystyle T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}r^{3}}{GM}T2=GM4π2r3​: r3=GMT24π2=3.98×1014×86 40024π2=7.53×1022 m3\displaystyle r^{3} = \frac{GMT^{2}}{4\pi^{2}} = \frac{3.98 \times 10^{14} \times 86\,400^{2}}{4\pi^{2}} = 7.53 \times 10^{22}\ \text{m}^{3}r3=4π2GMT2​=4π23.98×1014×864002​=7.53×1022 m3.
r=7.53×10223=4.2×107 m\displaystyle r = \sqrt[3]{7.53 \times 10^{22}} = 4.2 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}r=37.53×1022​=4.2×107 m

cards.q: State three features of a geostationary orbit.
cards.a: Its period is 24 hours, it is in the plane of the equator, and the satellite moves in the same direction as the Earth's rotation. It therefore stays above the same point on the Earth.

cards.q: Give one use of a geostationary satellite and one use of a satellite in low orbit.
cards.a: Geostationary: communications and television, because a fixed dish can point at it. Low orbit: imaging, weather and surveillance, because it is close to the surface and passes over all of it as the Earth turns beneath.

cards.q: Derive the expression for the escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass M\displaystyle MM and radius r\displaystyle rr.
cards.a: v=2GMr\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}v=r2GM​​
cards.why: The escape velocity does not depend on the mass of the object.
steps: To escape, the object must reach infinity, where its potential energy is zero.
Its kinetic energy at the surface must at least equal the gain in potential energy: 12mv2=GMmr\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{GMm}{r}21​mv2=rGMm​.
Cancel m\displaystyle mm: v=2GMr\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}v=r2GM​​.

cards.q: Calculate the escape velocity from the Earth's surface. (GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1\displaystyle GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}GM=3.98×1014 N m2 kg−1; radius 6.37×106 m\displaystyle 6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}6.37×106 m)
cards.a: 1.1×104 m s−1\displaystyle 1.1 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}1.1×104 m s−1
steps: v=2GMr=2×3.98×10146.37×106\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 3.98 \times 10^{14}}{6.37 \times 10^{6}}}v=r2GM​​=6.37×1062×3.98×1014​​
v=1.1×104 m s−1\displaystyle v = 1.1 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}v=1.1×104 m s−1

cards.q: For a satellite of mass m\displaystyle mm in a circular orbit of radius r\displaystyle rr, write its kinetic energy, its potential energy and its total energy.
cards.a: Kinetic: GMm2r\displaystyle \frac{GMm}{2r}2rGMm​. Potential: −GMmr\displaystyle -\frac{GMm}{r}−rGMm​. Total: −GMm2r\displaystyle -\frac{GMm}{2r}−2rGMm​.
cards.why: The total is negative: the satellite is bound to the planet.

cards.q: A satellite moves to a circular orbit of smaller radius. What happens to its speed, its potential energy and its total energy?
cards.a: Its speed increases, its potential energy decreases (becomes more negative), and its total energy decreases.
cards.why: It gains kinetic energy, but loses twice as much potential energy.

cards.q: Why do astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft feel weightless, although gravity still acts on them?
cards.a: The astronauts and the spacecraft are both in free fall, with the same acceleration towards the Earth. So the spacecraft exerts no contact force on them, and it is the contact force that gives the sensation of weight.

cards.q: Give two similarities and one difference between gravitational fields and electric fields.
cards.a: Similarities: both obey an inverse-square law for the force between point objects, and both can be described by field lines and by potential. Difference: gravity is always attractive, but electric forces can attract or repel.
